source_title: I Went to a Rave with Pikachu at Pokemon Night Out
source_excerpt:
Have you ever wanted to go to a rave with Pikachu?
Even as we inch closer to turning the page on 2026, The Pokemon Company isn’t ready to put a bow on its Pokemon 30th anniversary festivities just yet. Pokemon Night Out represents yet another celebration of the Pokemon brand, albeit in an unexpected form. GameRant was in attendance at the first leg of Pokemon Night Out, and admittedly, I was unsure what I was walking into. But by the end of the night, I left with a little ringing in my ears and a big smile on my face.
Pokemon chose Southern California’s Intuit Dome as its host for the US leg of the EDM tour. Home to the Los Angeles Clippers, the Intuit Dome is a state-of-the-art, brand-new stadium, with an intimidating, vertically oriented section dubbed “The Wall,” where fans look to distract free throw shooters with as much visual distraction as possible. For Pokemon Night Out, the stage sits in front of that wall, but what happens on that stage over the course of roughly 2 hours is just as much an assault on the senses.
Pokemon Night Out is billed as a fusion between electronic dance music (EDM) and Pokemon. But what exactly does that mean? With Marshmello as the headliner and Alison Wonderland as his opening act, the big-name quotient is sufficiently filled, but what type of show would they deliver?
As it turns out, Pokemon Night Out is an EDM show with Pokemon visuals. If you’re not a fan of that genre of music or you’re not at least casually familiar with Marshmello — maybe you've seen Marshmello in Fortnite — then you might not be as satisfied as someone whose Venn diagrams for Pokemon and EDM more overtly overlap. At one point during the show, Alison Wonderland does sample the Lavender Town theme for an EDM remix and the Pokemon TV show theme gets its moment, but a lot of the Pokemon connections in the show are visual in nature. Think of it like the visualizers you would see on a music video, only live and with a lot more going.
For Alison Wonderland, her visual elements were a little simpler. Familiar Pokemon were popping up in time with the beat/drop, and they always got a loud cheer from the crowd. Lights, lasers, and pyrotechnics further amplify the visual experience, but ultimately, the music is what drives everything. Alison Wonderland's fandom came through and that's what really endeared her performance to the crowd.
Marshmello’s stage setup is certainly more elaborate, with a massive, uniquely shaped screen. His booth is cut into the screen with visual elements behind him to make it seem like he is part of the on-screen action. The interplay between his DJ setup, the visuals on-screen, and the lasers, smoke, and pyrotechnics take what is otherwise a fairly straightforward listening experience and turns it into a true performance. At times, the Pokemon Night Out show used the screen simply to give a visual element to the music, but there were certain portions that utilized Pokemon to great effect.
For example, one sequence had Toxitricity rocking out with the beat, as if he were a guitarist amidst scaffolding. Another had the original Kanto starters walking on a moving globe with their final evolutions eventually accompanying them. And, of course, there was an entire Pikachu sequence that embraced the whimsy of the iconic Pokemon.
But three sections of Marshmello’s set sealed the deal for me. One featured a haunting backdrop that built to a really great moment with a massive Gengar. Another saw Pokemon Ruby and Sapphire cover stars Groudon and Kyogre duke it out in an epic battle. And my personal favorite used the song “Shockwave” to have Mewtwo assert his control over the show. That’s all I’ll say.
In addition to the Pokemon Night Out performances and some exclusive merch, there is also a Pokemon GO event that starts a few hours before and then lasts throughout almost the entire show. Raids with Pikachu and Gengar are live in a bunch of gyms, and there are two Timed Researches that unlock as well. Whether you get a shiny Pikachu, Gengar, or Toxitricity (from the research) is up to your luck, but all of them have a really cool nighttime background featuring the Los Angeles skyline or the London skyline if you’re at the November event.
I know that there is bound to be debate over whether Pokemon Night Out was more of an EDM show than a Pokemon celebration, but I think it bridged the gap really well. Pokemon was what got me in the door and kept me entertained, but I was also able to appreciate the stage presence of Alison Wonderland and Marshmello’s sets all on their own.
Pokemon Night Out now heads across the pond to London’s O2 Arena for another show.
